introduction_markdown: GENERAL CERTIFICATE OF EDUCATION BOARD, General Certificate of Education Examination. 0760 HISTORY 1, ADVANCED LEVEL, JUNE 2025. Multiple choice question paper. Duration: one and a half hours (1h 30). Instructions to candidates: use a soft HB pencil throughout the examination. Check that the question booklet is headed 'Advanced Level - 0760 History 1'. Answer ALL the 50 questions in this examination. All questions carry equal marks. Each question has FOUR suggested answers: A, B, C and D. Decide on which answer is correct and mark only one answer for each question (if you mark more than one answer you score zero for that question; if you change your mind, erase the first mark carefully). Avoid spending too much time on any one question: if a question is difficult, move on and come back to it later. Do all rough work in the booklet. Mobile phones are NOT allowed in the examination room.
incertitudes: Sujet scanné sans couche texte, lu en image (6 pages). La page de garde indique « History 1 », « 0760 », « JUNE 2025 », « ADVANCED LEVEL », « MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTION PAPER », durée une heure et demie ; 50 questions, aucune figure, carte ni document. Filigranes et mentions publicitaires (gcerevision.com, « KAWLO ») ignorés. Aucun point imprimé (toutes les questions comptent à égalité).

Aucun corrigé officiel n'est fourni : toutes les clés sont déduites de l'historiographie usuelle (manuels camerounais d'histoire, programme du GCE) et n'ont pas pu être confrontées à un barème officiel.

Faits historiques énoncés avec prudence dans les corrigés, non vérifiables ici faute de source : Q2 (succession matrilinéaire chez les Kom et les Aghem), Q9 (détail des révoltes Duala, Gbaya et Bamoum sous le mandat français, sans dates précises), Q10 (contenu exact de la Constitution Macpherson de 1951 pour le Southern Cameroons : sièges à l'Eastern House of Assembly, place dans l'Executive Council), Q14 (positions des délégations à Foumban, monnaie CFA laissée à des mesures ultérieures), Q15 (rôle de S.T. Muna et de A.N. Jua dans la naissance du CUC en 1965), Q17 (disparition de la West Cameroon House of Chiefs ; hausse de salaire des fonctionnaires de l'Ouest non vérifiable), Q19 (ordre des événements de la rupture Ahidjo-Biya), Q20 (rétablissement des relations avec Israël au milieu des années 1980, visite du pape en 1985). Aucune statistique ni citation inventée.

Neuf QCM ont été convertis en questions ouvertes parce que deux options au moins sont défendables, que l'énoncé est ambigu ou que le fait ne peut pas être vérifié ici : 5 (changement de politique britannique en 1884 : progrès du commerce allemand, rapports sur les contacts germano-chefs côtiers ou pression des Baptistes, réponse visée A), 11 (facteur déterminant du nationalisme au Cameroun français : Brazzaville, USCC, hostilité à la politique coloniale ou création de l'UPC ; réponse visée C), 12 (victoire du KNDP en 1959 : option B retenue comme exception, non vérifiée), 13 (opposition de l'UPC à l'option d'Ahidjo en 1958 : élections avant l'indépendance, option C, ou absence de la réunification, option B), 15 (création du CUC en 1965 : crise du KNDP, renvoi de Muna ou nomination de Jua, options qui se recouvrent ; réponse visée B), 17 (référendum de 1972 : l'option C est fausse mais l'option D n'est pas vérifiable ; réponse visée C), 25 (facteur « naturel » de l'échec de Samori Touré : seule l'option A est géographique, mais « strategic location » suggère un avantage ; réponse visée A), 39 (changement de la politique de Bismarck après 1871 : isolement de la France, option A, ou Triple Alliance, option C ; réponse visée C), 49 (persistance de la guerre israélo-arabe : occupation de terres arabes, option B, ou soutien occidental à Israël, option C ; réponse visée B).

QCM conservés avec une clé défendable mais moins sûre : Q1 (C : la redistribution de la population ; A « séparation des familles » reste discutable), Q9 (A : la politique de l'indigénat comme provocation commune), Q16 (C : « carrot and stick »), Q18 (A : production vivrière et animale), Q19 (A : qui définit les orientations de la politique nationale ; C et D sont des étapes de l'escalade), Q27 (A : préservation des institutions traditionnelles ; B décrit la méthode plus que l'effet), Q29 (A : effets de la Seconde Guerre mondiale, indice « after 1945 »), Q31 (C : mépris français pour l'islam, cause sociale ; A est plutôt économique), Q42 (A : création de la Société des Nations, réponse de manuel ; C est défendable), Q44 (B : pacte germano-soviétique comme déclencheur immédiat ; D est défendable), Q50 (B : diplomatie du ping-pong).

Défauts du sujet imprimé : Q33 « 1965 presidential election crisis » : le Nigeria n'avait pas d'élection présidentielle en 1965 (il s'agit vraisemblablement des élections régionales de l'Ouest d'octobre 1965) ; la clé D est retenue parce que la formulation imprimée la rend fausse, mais si le sujet visait l'élection régionale, la question n'aurait aucune exception ; Q41 « Japan withdrew prematurely » : historiquement le Japon a menacé de partir et a finalement signé, c'est l'Italie qui a quitté la conférence à cause de Fiume ; Q36 « re-enactment of the Habeas Corpus Act » : la loi date de 1679, ce que 1688-1689 confirme n'est qu'indirect ; Q25 « natural factor » : aucune option n'est clairement naturelle ; Q40 « liberation of occupied territories » est ambigu (la perte de l'Alsace-Lorraine peut se dire libération côté français), clé B retenue par élimination ; Fautes d'impression : Q10 « Lyttleton » (Lyttelton), Q30 « Kikiyu » (Kikuyu), Q15 « A.N.Jua » (espace manquant), Q33 option C « the1964 » (espace manquant), Q41 « the reject of claims », Q9 « requesting for self-government », Q11 « polices » (policies) ; les espaces manquantes et l'orthographe de Kikuyu sont corrigées dans la transcription, les autres fautes (dont « Lyttleton ») sont conservées telles qu'imprimées. La numérotation des instructions de la page de garde saute de 10 à 12 (point 11 absent), sans incidence.

Un seul fichier : Paper 1, un exercice de 50 questions, aucune section, aucune règle de choix (toutes les questions sont obligatoires). Les clés ne sont pas confrontées à une clé officielle : toute option notée « Intended answer » dans une question ouverte reste une réponse visée, pas une certitude.

Seconde passe faite page par page : énoncés et options relus un à un contre le scan, puis chaque question refaite indépendamment (voir les clés retenues ci-dessus) ; faits cités dans les corrigés rédigés avec prudence ; aucune statistique ni citation inventée.
Converties en questions ouvertes par le relecteur (clé ou options discutables) : 5, 11, 12, 13, 15, 17, 25, 39, 49.

questions.enonce_markdown: The most important social effect of population movements in Cameroon during the 19th century was the
questions.corrige_markdown: In the 19th century wars, the Fulani advance and the search for land set many groups moving within and into the territory of present-day Cameroon. The lasting social result was that the population of the territory was redistributed: peoples settled in new areas, mixed with earlier inhabitants and produced the pattern of settlement that the Europeans found at the end of the century. Separation of families (A) and the abandonment of ancestral sites (B) were costs of the movements rather than their main lasting result, and the spread of Islam (D) was a religious effect felt only in some areas. The wording "social effect" leaves A somewhat defensible, but C is the most general and most lasting effect. **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: separation of families.
abandonment of ancestral sites.
redistribution of Cameroon's population.
spread of Islam in the Western Grassland.

questions.enonce_markdown: The matrilineal system of succession in the pre-colonial states and kingdoms of the Bamenda Grassfields was commonly practiced by the
questions.corrige_markdown: In a matrilineal system the throne and property pass through the female line (to the ruler's sister's son or a member of the mother's lineage). In the Bamenda Grassfields this system is typical of Kom and Aghem. Mankon, Bafut, Nso, Bali, Nkwen and Bamendankwe passed the throne from father to son (patrilineal succession), so options B, C and D are wrong. **Answer: A.**
themes: pre-colonial peoples and states of cameroon

choix.texte: Kom and Aghem.
Mankon and Bafut.
Nso and Bali.
Nkwen and Bamendankwe.

questions.enonce_markdown: The Jihads in Northern Cameroon can be considered as barbaric because
questions.corrige_markdown: To call the jihads barbaric is to point to their violence and its human cost. The destruction of farmlands and settlements (D) is such a cost: villages were burnt, crops were lost and many people were killed or enslaved. A change in land tenure (A) is an administrative change, the end of extortion (B) would be a benefit and not a barbarity, and the defeat of rulers (C) is a military result which says nothing in itself about cruelty. **Answer: D.**
themes: fulani jihads in west africa and cameroon

choix.texte: the land tenure system was changed.
the system of extortion came to an end.
the Kirdi rulers were defeated at Mandara.
many farmlands and settlements were destroyed.

questions.enonce_markdown: The most immediate factor that favoured the implantation of the London Baptist Mission in Cameroon was
questions.corrige_markdown: The Baptist Missionary Society (London) had worked on the island of Fernando Po (Bioko) under Alfred Saker. When the Spanish authorities, who allowed only Catholic worship, forced the Protestant missionaries to leave in 1858, Saker and a group of his converts settled on the mainland coast of Cameroon and founded Victoria on Ambas Bay. The eviction from Fernando Po (D) was therefore the immediate factor. The founding of Victoria (C) was the implantation itself, not a factor favouring it; the failure of the Niger Expedition (A, 1841) and the anti-slave trade campaigns (B) belong to the wider background. **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: the failure of the Niger Expedition.
the anti-slave trade campaigns.
the founding of Victoria in 1858.
the eviction of the Baptist missionaries from Fernando Po.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The primary reason for the change of policy by Britain in April 1884 in favour of the annexation of Cameroon was

*Options as printed:* A) the rapid progress of German trade in the area.   B) the British intelligence reports on the secret meetings between the Germans and the coastal chiefs.   C) the French policy of trade protectionism.   D) the pressure from the London Baptist Missionary Society.
questions.corrige_markdown:
For years Britain had left unanswered the requests of the Duala chiefs for protection. In 1884 its attitude changed because German commercial houses (such as Woermann) were gaining ground on the coast and Germany was turning to colonial expansion, which threatened British trade. The consul Edward Hewett was sent to make treaties, but he reached the coast a few days after Gustav Nachtigal had obtained the German treaty with the Duala chiefs (July 1884). The key retained here is A (the rapid progress of German trade), but the pressure of British traders and of the Baptist mission (D) and the reports on German contacts with the chiefs (B) are also cited by textbooks. The French policy of protectionism (C) is not usually given as the reason for the change.

**Intended answer: A (the rapid progress of German trade in the area).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: Indigenous resistance against the Germans in Cameroon was induced by the following grievances EXCEPT
questions.corrige_markdown: German rule was resented for forced labour on plantations, roads and railways (B), for public flogging and other corporal punishment (D), and for ignoring local customs and the authority of chiefs (A). The administration did not impose Christianity: the missions (Basel, Catholic, Baptist) worked alongside it and conversion remained voluntary. Option C is therefore the exception. **Answer: C.**
themes: indigenous resistance to german rule in cameroon

choix.texte: the violation of indigenous customs and traditions.
the imposition of forced labour.
the imposition of Christian religion.
public flogging of indigenous people.

questions.enonce_markdown: The early capture of Douala was significant to the victory of the Allied powers during the First World war in Cameroon in that
questions.corrige_markdown: Douala, the main port and the terminus of the German railways, was taken by Anglo-French forces in September 1914. Its fall closed the main entry point of the colony, so the German forces were cut off from supplies and reinforcements coming by sea (D). It did not end the war (B): the German resistance lasted until early 1916, when the last troops withdrew to Spanish Guinea. The Germans were not prevented from retreating (C), since they withdrew inland towards Yaounde and later out of the colony, and the capture had nothing to do with neutralising the support of two peoples (A). **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: it neutralised the Duala and the Ewondo support.
it led to the victory of the Allies and the end of war.
it prevented the retreat of German soldiers.
it sealed off the Cameroon coast from German supplies.

questions.enonce_markdown: Both Britain and France strictly conformed to the following Mandate terms EXCEPT
questions.corrige_markdown: Under Article 22 of the Covenant of the League of Nations and the Mandate agreements, the mandatory powers had to send annual reports (A), guarantee freedom of conscience and worship (B) and respect local laws and customs (D). The agreements forbade the militarization of the territory: no military bases and no military training of the inhabitants except for police and local defence. "Complete militarization" (C) is therefore the term that Britain and France did not conform to. **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: the submission of annual reports to the League of Nations.
the exercise of complete freedom of conscience and worship.
the complete militarization of both territories.
the respect for indigenous laws and customs.

questions.enonce_markdown: The Duala, Gbaya and Bamum revolts against French administration during the Mandate period were similar in that
questions.corrige_markdown: Under the Mandate the French applied the indigenat, a set of summary penalties for "natives", together with forced labour and compulsory recruitment. The Gbaya revolt of the late 1920s (Karnou) was triggered by forced labour and recruitment for railway works, the Bamum king Njoya came into conflict with the French administration and was removed in the early 1930s, and Duala protests also denounced the treatment of Africans by the administration. The common provocation is therefore the abuses of the indigenat system (A). Land expropriation (D) concerns the Duala only; cash crop imposition (B) and a demand for self-government (C) do not describe all three movements. The key is the best fit but is less certain than for other questions. **Answer: A.**
themes: revolts in french cameroon under the mandate

choix.texte: they were provoked by the French Policy of Indigenat.
they were against the imposition of cash crop cultivation.
they were requesting for self-government.
they were triggered by land expropriation.

questions.enonce_markdown: An important constitutional change in the 1950s which granted Southern Cameroons representation in both the Legislative and Executive Councils of Eastern Nigeria was
questions.corrige_markdown: The Macpherson Constitution of 1951 introduced regional legislatures and executive councils in Nigeria, and Southern Cameroons, then administered as part of the Eastern Region, received seats in the Eastern House of Assembly and a place in the Region's Executive Council. The Richards Constitution (B) dates from 1946, not from the 1950s; the Clifford Constitution (D) dates from 1922 and concerned the Legislative Council of Nigeria; the Lyttelton Constitution (C, 1954) went further and gave Southern Cameroons a quasi-federal status with its own House of Assembly, which is a different change. **Answer: A.**

choix.texte: the Macpherson Constitution.
the Richards Constitution.
the Lyttleton Constitution.
the Clifford Constitution.

questions.enonce_markdown:
A significant determining factor for the growth of nationalism in French Cameroon was

*Options as printed:* A) the convening of the Brazzaville Conference of 1944.   B) the formation of USCC.   C) the dislike for French colonial polices.   D) the creation of the Union des Populations du Cameroun (UPC).
questions.corrige_markdown:
French rule, first under the Mandate and then under the Trusteeship, brought forced labour, the indigenat (abolished only in 1946), unequal political rights and economic hardship. Resentment of these colonial policies spread widely and gave nationalism its mass support. The Brazzaville Conference of 1944 (A) promised limited reforms, the trade union USCC (B, formed in 1944) trained leaders and the UPC (D, founded in April 1948) gave the movement an organisation; they channelled the discontent more than they caused it, but each of them can be argued as a factor.

**Intended answer: C (the dislike for French colonial polices).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The KNDP victory in the 1959 elections in the Southern Cameroons was the product of the following factors EXCEPT

*Options as printed:* A) the disunity within the KNC-KPP Alliance.   B) the support of French Cameroon politicians to the KNDP.   C) the support of traditional authorities to the KNDP.   D) the flexible campaign strategy of the KNDP.
questions.corrige_markdown:
In the January 1959 elections J. N. Foncha's KNDP defeated the KNC-KPP Alliance led by E. M. L. Endeley. The usual explanations are the weakness and disunity of the Alliance (A), the backing of many Grassfields chiefs and traditional authorities (C) and a campaign that left room for several constitutional futures instead of a single fixed stand (D). Support from the politicians of French Cameroon (B) is not among the factors normally listed, so B is the intended exception; the printed question cannot be checked against a source here.

**Intended answer: B (the support of French Cameroon politicians to the KNDP).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Ahidjo's option of independence for French Cameroon at the UN General Assembly in 1958 was strongly challenged by the UPC party because

*Options as printed:* A) the UPC leader, Um Nyobe, was assassinated.   B) Ahidjo did not include reunification in his program of independence.   C) the UPC wanted elections before independence.   D) the UPC wanted independence for British Southern Cameroons.
questions.corrige_markdown:
At the United Nations in 1958 the UPC, banned in 1955 and led from exile by Felix Moumie after the death of Ruben Um Nyobe in September 1958, opposed the plan of independence on 1 January 1960 under the government of Ahmadou Ahidjo. It asked for amnesty and for general elections held before independence, so that a government with a real popular mandate would receive it, and it also demanded reunification with British Cameroons. Option C is retained as the intended answer, but B is also defensible, and Um Nyobe's death (A) was a grievance, not a reason against the plan.

**Intended answer: C (the UPC wanted elections before independence).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: The most important outcome of the Foumban Constitutional Conference of July 1961 to French Cameroonians was
questions.corrige_markdown: At Foumban the delegation of East Cameroon came with a draft which favoured strong central powers, while the Southern Cameroons delegates had hoped for a loose federation with strong states. The conference ended with a federal constitution in which the Federal Government held wide powers, an arrangement that served the interests of East Cameroon (French Cameroonians). The preservation of the two legal systems (C) was rather a guarantee for Southern Cameroons, and monetary arrangements (D) were settled by later measures. **Answer: B.**

choix.texte: the adoption of a single nationality.
the adoption of a strong centralised federal government.
that English and French legal systems were to be preserved.
the CFA franc became a legal tender.

questions.enonce_markdown:
In 1965, the CUC political party was created in West Cameroon mainly because of

*Options as printed:* A) the dismissal of S.T. Muna from the KNDP.   B) the KNDP political crisis.   C) the appointment of A.N. Jua as Prime Minister.   D) the coalition between the KNDP and CPNC.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The Cameroon United Congress (CUC) was formed in 1965 by dissidents from the KNDP, among them S. T. Muna, after the split in the ruling party of West Cameroon. The underlying cause was the crisis in the KNDP (B), which included the rivalry around Muna and the change of Prime Minister from Foncha to A. N. Jua in 1965 (A and C are parts of that crisis). The coalition with the CPNC (D) belongs to another political episode. The key is retained as B, but the printed options overlap and the precise role of each event could not be checked.

**Intended answer: B (the KNDP political crisis).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: The most successful approach used by Ahidjo to silence his political opponents in East Cameroon in the 1960s was through
questions.corrige_markdown: Ahidjo combined rewards and punishments. The "carrot" was positions in the government and the party, honours and favours for opponents who rallied to him; the "stick" was arrest, detention and the banning of those who refused. This policy led the opposition parties to merge into a single party, the Cameroon National Union (CNU, 1966). Control of the press (A), police repression (B) and control of the judiciary (D) were instruments of the "stick" only, and they were less successful alone because they did not win over the leaders of the opposition. **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: the strict control of the press.
the oppression by the police.
the "carrot and stick" diplomacy.
the control of the judiciary.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The following were the results of the 1972 referendum EXCEPT

*Options as printed:* A) the abolition of the post of Vice President.   B) the creation of a National Assembly with 120 deputies.   C) the West Cameroon House of Chiefs was maintained.   D) the increase in the salary of West Cameroon civil servants.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The referendum of 20 May 1972 approved a unitary state, and the United Republic of Cameroon was proclaimed on 2 June 1972. The federal structure disappeared: the post of Vice President (A) was abolished, a single National Assembly of 120 deputies was created (B), and the institutions of the federated states, including the West Cameroon House of Chiefs, did not survive. The statement that the House of Chiefs was maintained (C) is therefore false and is the exception. The claim about a salary increase for West Cameroon civil servants (D) could not be checked, which is why this question is not safe to mark automatically.

**Intended answer: C (the West Cameroon House of Chiefs was maintained).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
themes: creation of the united republic of cameroon

questions.enonce_markdown: President Ahmadou Ahidjo launched the Green Revolution in Buea in 1973 with the main objective of
questions.corrige_markdown: The Green Revolution launched at Buea in 1973 was a programme to modernise agriculture and raise the production of food crops and livestock, so that the country would feed itself and reduce rural-urban migration. Jobs (B) and agricultural shows (C) were means or by-products, and the promotion of primary industries (D) is too general and not the stated aim. **Answer: A.**

choix.texte: increasing food and livestock production in Cameroon.
creating job opportunities for Cameroonians.
organising Agro-Pastoral Shows.
promoting primary industries.

questions.enonce_markdown: The main cause of the rift between Ahidjo and Biya in the 1980s was
questions.corrige_markdown: Ahidjo resigned as President in November 1982 but stayed at the head of the ruling party, the CNU, and expected to keep deciding the main lines of national policy, whereas Biya, as Head of State, claimed that power. This dispute over who defined the nation's policy is the root of the rift (A). The cabinet reshuffle of June 1983 (C) and Ahidjo's call to Northern ministers (D) were steps in the escalation of the quarrel, not its root. The key retained is A, but the order of the events could not be checked against a source. **Answer: A.**

choix.texte: the differences over who defines the guidelines of the nation's policy.
Biya's declaration that no one tribe had a monopoly of power.
the cabinet reshuffle of June 1983.
Ahidjo's call for Northern Ministers in Biya's government to resign.

questions.enonce_markdown: The following were major shifts in Cameroon's foreign policy since the advent of the New Deal regime in 1982 EXCEPT
questions.corrige_markdown: Under President Biya's New Deal, Cameroon moved towards closer ties with Israel (diplomatic relations broken in the early 1970s were restored in the mid-1980s), with the Vatican (Pope John Paul II visited Cameroon in 1985) and towards wider international cooperation. The special relationship with France was not a shift: it already existed under Ahidjo and continued. Option A is therefore the exception. **Answer: A.**

choix.texte: special ties with France.
close ties with the state of Israel.
close ties with the Vatican.
increased international cooperation.

questions.enonce_markdown: The most important strategy that greatly contributed to the success of the British campaigns against slave trade in West Africa in the 19th century was
questions.corrige_markdown: Laws such as the Abolition Act of 1807 made the trade illegal for British subjects, but they could be enforced at sea only by ships. The West Africa Squadron of the Royal Navy patrolled the coast from 1808 onwards, stopped slave ships and freed the captives, which made the campaign effective. Compensation (A) was paid to slave owners, not traders, and later; Sierra Leone (D) was a home for freed slaves, not a means of enforcement. **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: the payment of compensation to slave traders.
the enactment of abolition laws by Parliament.
the deployment of a British naval squadron to West Africa.
the founding of Sierra Leone.

questions.enonce_markdown: A significant social contribution of the Church Missionary Society in Sierra Leone was
questions.corrige_markdown: The Church Missionary Society (CMS) founded Fourah Bay College at Freetown in 1827 to train teachers, clergy and catechists. It became the first centre of higher education in West Africa and a lasting social and educational contribution. The other options are not specific achievements of the CMS: peace and stability were the business of the colonial government, and crafts and agriculture were not its main legacy. **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: the maintenance of peace and stability.
the establishment of small scale industries in craft.
the promotion of agriculture.
the creation of the Fourah Bay College.

questions.enonce_markdown: A positive religious impact of the 19th century Jihads in West Africa was that it led to
questions.corrige_markdown: The 19th century jihads (Usman dan Fodio, Al-Hajj Umar and others) were reform movements which aimed to remove pagan practices from the Islam of the region and to apply Islamic law more strictly. The purification of Islam (B) is therefore the religious impact. Fulani hegemony (A) is a political result, and the expansion of trade (C) and the caravan routes (D) are economic results. **Answer: B.**

choix.texte: the establishment of Fulani hegemony.
the purification of Islam.
the expansion of trade.
the establishment of caravan trade routes.

questions.enonce_markdown: The European scramble for African territories in the 19th century was motivated by the following factors EXCEPT
questions.corrige_markdown: The scramble had economic motives (raw materials and markets, C), strategic motives (naval bases on the sea routes, D) and political motives such as rivalry between the powers, prestige and the wish to keep the European balance of power (B). Political instability in Europe is not among the usual causes; the scramble was driven by competition between stable states. Option A is therefore the exception. **Answer: A.**

choix.texte: political instability in Europe.
the desire to maintain European balance of power.
the quest for raw materials.
the search for strategic naval bases.

questions.enonce_markdown:
A natural factor that contributed to the failure of Samori Toure's resistance was

*Options as printed:* A) the strategic location of the Mandinka Empire.   B) the French military superiority.   C) the absence of strategic defence.   D) the prolonged nature of the war.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Samori Toure's empire lay in the interior of West Africa, far from the coast, which made it difficult to import arms and to find allies, and its position between the French, the British in Sierra Leone and Liberia left him little room to retreat. Of the four options, only the location (A) is a geographical, that is natural, factor; French military superiority (B) and the absence of strategic defence (C) are military and human factors, and the length of the war (D) is a circumstance. The wording "strategic location" suggests an advantage, so the question is ambiguous and the key is retained with reserve.

**Intended answer: A (the strategic location of the Mandinka Empire).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: The ineffectiveness of African resistance to European conquest and occupation after 1885 was the product of the following factors EXCEPT
questions.corrige_markdown: African resistance was weakened by beliefs in the protection of charms in battle (A), by divisions between peoples which the Europeans exploited (B) and by the effects of the slave trade, which had weakened and divided societies (C). The mastery of the terrain was an advantage of the Africans, which helped them in some battles; it cannot explain their failure. Option D is therefore the exception. **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: African superstitious beliefs in warfare.
the lack of unity among Africans.
the impact of slave trade on the Africans.
the mastery of the terrain by African soldiers.

questions.enonce_markdown: The most important positive impact of the British policy of Indirect Rule in her West African colonies was
questions.corrige_markdown: Indirect Rule (associated with Lord Lugard) governed through the existing chiefs and emirs. Its most important positive effect was that traditional institutions, rulers and customs were kept alive and respected. The use of traditional authorities in administration (B) is the method of the policy itself, not its impact; ethnic revolts were not prevented (C), as shown by protests such as the Women's War of 1929 in south-eastern Nigeria, and self-reliance (D) was not an aim of the policy. **Answer: A.**

choix.texte: the preservation of traditional institutions and culture.
the use of traditional authorities in administration.
the prevention of ethnic revolts.
the promotion of the culture of self-reliance development.

questions.enonce_markdown: The main reason for the extension of World War II to Africa was
questions.corrige_markdown: Africa lay on key sea routes (the Mediterranean, the Suez Canal and the Cape route), had raw materials and bases, and bordered the Italian and Vichy French possessions. For this reason both sides fought for control of it, in North Africa, East Africa and the Atlantic coast. The liberation of Ethiopia (A) was only one operation, the recruitment of African soldiers (C) was a consequence of the war, and the second front in Europe (D) was opened in Normandy in 1944, not as a reason for fighting in Africa. **Answer: B.**
themes: impact of world war two on africa

choix.texte: the desire to liberate Ethiopia.
the strategic importance of Africa.
the need to recruit African soldiers.
the need to open a second front in Europe.

questions.enonce_markdown: A driving force behind the rapid growth of African nationalism after 1945 was
questions.corrige_markdown: After 1945 the Second World War changed the situation: the colonial powers were weakened, African ex-servicemen returned with new ideas and experience, the Atlantic Charter and the United Nations promoted self-determination, and the war had caused economic hardship. These effects (A) are the driving force that turned older protest into rapid growth after 1945. The elite (B), colonial abuses (C) and the press (D) also played a part, but they were present before 1945, so they do not explain the sudden acceleration; the choice of A is reasoned but not certain. **Answer: A.**

choix.texte: the effects of the Second World War.
the activities of the elite.
the ills of colonial rule.
the contributions of the press.

questions.enonce_markdown: The main economic grievance that influenced the Mau Mau rebellion in Kenya in the 1950s against British colonial administration was
questions.corrige_markdown: The Mau Mau rebellion (from 1952) was mainly a Kikuyu revolt against the loss of land to white settlers in the Kenya highlands, which left many Kikuyu landless or working as squatters. The expropriation of Kikuyu lands (A) is therefore the main economic grievance. Taxes (B) and cash crops (D) were not its core issue, and the expulsion of settlers (C) was an aim of the rebels, not a grievance. **Answer: A.**

choix.texte: the expropriation of Kikuyu lands.
the imposition of arbitrary taxes.
the expulsion of white settlers.
the imposition of cash crop cultivation.

questions.enonce_markdown: A social cause of the Algerian War of Independence was
questions.corrige_markdown: The war which began in 1954 had economic causes (the loss of land to European settlers, A), political causes and social causes. The French contempt for Islam and for the cultural practices of Algerians, together with the unequal social status of Muslims, is a social cause (C). The occupation of land (A) is mainly an economic cause. The construction of European schools (B) was an instrument of assimilation but not a typical grievance, and the Malikite code (D) is a school of Islamic law, not something imposed by the French. **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: the French occupation of indigenous land.
the construction of European schools in Algeria.
the French contempt for Islam and its practices.
the imposition of the Malikite Code in Algeria.

questions.enonce_markdown: The following were negative manifestations of Neo-colonialism in former French Equatorial African colonies EXCEPT
questions.corrige_markdown: After independence France kept strong influence in Gabon, Chad, the Central African Republic and Congo through the choice of friendly leaders (A), military bases and interventions (B) and economic control of resources and trade (D). The promotion of democratic governance (C) is a positive aim, not a negative manifestation, and it was not the usual result of French influence. Option C is the exception. **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: the imposition of political leaders.
frequent military interventions.
promotion of democratic governance.
French economic exploitation.

questions.enonce_markdown: The January 1966 military coup d'etat in Nigeria was attributed to the following political events EXCEPT
questions.corrige_markdown: The January 1966 coup, led by young army officers, followed the crisis in the Western Region in 1962 (A), the dispute over the 1963 census (B), the troubled federal elections of December 1964 (C), and the violent Western Region elections of October 1965. Nigeria had no presidential election in 1965 (the President was a ceremonial head of state, chosen by Parliament), so D describes an event which did not take place and is the exception. It is likely that the question means the 1965 regional election in the West; if so the question has no exception, and this is noted in the uncertainties. **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: the 1962 political crisis in the West.
the 1963 population census crisis.
the 1964 federal election crisis.
the 1965 presidential election crisis.

questions.enonce_markdown: February 1990 marked a turning point in the fight against Apartheid in South Africa because of
questions.corrige_markdown: Nelson Mandela was released from prison on 11 February 1990, after the government of F. W. de Klerk had lifted the ban on the ANC and other organisations. This opened the negotiations which led to the end of apartheid. The Soweto uprising (A) dates from 1976, the Sharpeville massacre (C) from 1960, and Mandela was elected President only in 1994 (B). **Answer: D.**

the election of Nelson Mandela as first Black President.
the Sharpville Massacre.
the release of Nelson Mandela from prison.

questions.enonce_markdown: An outstanding negative impact of refugees in the departure countries was
questions.corrige_markdown: The question asks about the countries which the refugees leave (the countries of origin). There the main negative impact is depopulation (C): many people, often the young and the skilled, leave and the labour force and the economy are weakened. Tension with local people (A), food shortages (B) and pressure on social amenities (D) are the problems of the host countries. **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: the tension between refugees and the local population.
food shortages.
depopulation.
increased pressure on social amenities.

questions.enonce_markdown: The following were 'glorious' outcomes of the English Revolution of 1688 EXCEPT
questions.corrige_markdown: The revolution (William III and Mary II replacing James II) was called glorious because it was bloodless and because it brought the supremacy of Parliament over the Crown (B), the Bill of Rights of 1689 confirming the rights of subjects, which includes the protection of liberty associated with Habeas Corpus (A), and the victory of the Protestant Anglican Church over Catholicism (D). The Crown lost powers such as suspending laws and raising taxes without Parliament, so the maintenance of Royal patronage (C) was not an outcome and is the exception. **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: the re-enactment of the Habeas Corpus Act.
the triumph of Parliament over the Crown.
the maintenance of Royal patronage.
the triumph of Anglicanism over Catholicism.

questions.enonce_markdown: An outstanding political impact of the American Revolution on America was
questions.corrige_markdown: The question asks for the political impact on America itself. The Declaration of 1776, recognised by Britain at the Treaty of Paris of 1783, created the independent United States (A), a republic with its own constitution. The French Revolution (B) and the fall of Lord North in 1782 (C) are effects on Europe and Britain, and the search for new colonies (D) concerns Britain. **Answer: A.**

choix.texte: the independence of the USA.
the outbreak of the French Revolution.
the resignation of the British Prime Minister, Lord North.
the British search for new colonies.

questions.enonce_markdown: Britain influenced the collapse of the Congress System by
questions.corrige_markdown: The Congress System, set up after the Napoleonic wars, wanted the great powers to act together to put down revolutions. Britain, first under Castlereagh (State Paper of 1820) and then under Canning, refused to take part in the collective suppression of revolutions in other countries (D), and this opposition weakened the system. Britain did not intervene itself to suppress revolts (A); the slave trade (B) and piracy (C) were not the cause of the collapse. **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: intervening and suppressing revolts in Europe.
promoting the abolition of slave trade.
stamping out piracy in the Mediterranean Sea.
opposing the collective suppression of revolutions.

questions.enonce_markdown:
A major shift in Bismarck's foreign policy in Europe after 1871 was witnessed in

*Options as printed:* A) the isolation of France.   B) the convening of the Berlin West Africa Conference.   C) the formation of the Triple Alliance.   D) the entry into the colonial race.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Before 1871 Bismarck made wars to unify Germany; after 1871 he wanted to keep the peace and protect the new empire by a system of alliances. The Triple Alliance (C, 1882: Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy) was the best known result of this change. The isolation of France (A) was an aim of the policy that continued throughout, the Berlin Conference of 1884-1885 (B) and the entry into the colonial race (D) concern Africa and not Europe. The question is ambiguous between A and C.

**Intended answer: C (the formation of the Triple Alliance).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: The following were negative results of the First World War on Germany EXCEPT
questions.corrige_markdown: The Treaty of Versailles (1919) limited the German army to 100,000 men (A), took away her colonies, which became mandates (C), and imposed reparations (D). The end of the German occupation of Belgium and northern France (B) was a consequence of the defeat and a condition of the armistice, not a penalty imposed on Germany by the settlement, and it is not counted among the harmful results; B is the exception. **Answer: B.**

the liberation of occupied territories.
the loss of colonial possessions.
the payment of reparations.

questions.enonce_markdown: Japan withdrew prematurely from the Paris Peace Conference in April 1919 because of the following reasons EXCEPT
questions.corrige_markdown: At Paris, Japan asked for the former German rights in Shantung (A and D), and for a clause on racial equality in the Covenant of the League of Nations (B). Fiume was a port claimed by Italy, not by Japan; Italy left the conference in April 1919 when Fiume was refused. The rejection of demands over Fiume (C) is therefore not a reason for the Japanese attitude and is the exception. (Historically Japan threatened to leave but finally stayed, so the statement of the question is loose.) **Answer: C.**

the refusal of racial equality with Europeans.

questions.enonce_markdown: The greatest achievement of the Paris Peace Settlement (1919-1923) was
questions.corrige_markdown: The settlement produced the Treaties of Versailles, Saint-Germain, Trianon, Neuilly and Sevres/Lausanne. Its most original and ambitious achievement was the creation of the League of Nations (A), the first permanent world organisation for peace and cooperation. Disarmament (B) concerned only the defeated states, self-determination (C) was applied only partly, in Europe, and the minority problems (D) were not resolved but created new ones. The key follows the usual textbook answer. **Answer: A.**

choix.texte: the creation of the League of Nations.
the disarmament of some European nations.
the granting of self-determination to the oppressed peoples.
the resolution of minority problems.

questions.enonce_markdown: A structural weakness of the League of Nations which influenced its failure was
questions.corrige_markdown: A structural weakness is a defect in the organisation itself. The League had no army of its own and depended on its members to apply sanctions or to send troops, which they were unwilling to do (A). The Great Depression (B), American isolationism (C) and the aggression of dictators (D) were external circumstances, not defects in the structure of the League. **Answer: A.**

choix.texte: the lack of a standing army to enforce its decisions.
the effects of the Great Depression.
the American policy of Isolationism.
the contributions of dictators.

questions.enonce_markdown: The outbreak of the Second World War in 1939 was precipitated by
questions.corrige_markdown: To precipitate is to bring about immediately. In August 1939 the Nazi-Soviet Non-aggression Pact removed the danger of a war on two fronts for Hitler and secretly divided Poland between the two powers; the German attack on Poland followed within a week and led Britain and France to declare war (B). The collapse of collective security (A) was a long-term cause, the remilitarisation of the Rhineland (C, 1936) a distant step, and the occupation of Czechoslovakia (D, March 1939) an earlier event which ended appeasement and can also be argued. **Answer: B.**

the Nazi-Soviet Non-aggression Pact.

questions.enonce_markdown: As used by Winston Churchill in 1946, the Iron Curtain signifies
questions.corrige_markdown: In his speech at Fulton, Missouri (March 1946), Churchill said that an "iron curtain" had descended across Europe, from the Baltic to the Adriatic, separating the Western countries from the Soviet-controlled Eastern Europe. an imaginary line dividing Europe into Capitalist and Communist Blocs.

questions.enonce_markdown: A major effect of the Korean War on the functioning of the UNO was
questions.corrige_markdown: During the Korean War (1950-1953) the Soviet veto threatened to paralyse the Security Council. The Soviet boycott of the Security Council (C) took place in early 1950, over the Chinese seat, before the war began, and the People's Republic of China was not then a member of the UN; the repeated use of the veto (B) was already a feature of the UN since 1946; and the division at the 38th Parallel (D) dates from 1945. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The persistence of wars in the Middle East between Israel and the Arabs since 1948 has been attributed to

*Options as printed:* A) increasing Arab nationalism.   B) Israeli occupation of Arab lands.   C) Western support to Israel.   D) Israeli military strength.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The wars of 1948, 1956, 1967 and 1973 and the later conflicts kept going mainly because of disputes over territory: the Israeli occupation of Arab lands (Sinai, Gaza, the West Bank, the Golan Heights and East Jerusalem after 1967) has remained an obstacle to peace. B is the intended answer. Western support to Israel (C), Arab nationalism (A) and Israeli military strength (D) are also given as factors, so the question is not safe to mark automatically.
